questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
In my case, I selected Bangor University strictly from an academic point of view. One of my professors at University of Copenhagen had discussed an idea I had for my Master's thesis topic back in March 2022. During our discussions he had mentioned a professor that works at Bangor University that he had previously worked with, that would is specifically specialized in the topic I was researching.  I had gotten in contact with this professor by April 2022 and they were more than willing to collaborate with me on my thesis as a supervisor (and they are now (still), officially supervising me on my thesis).

Furthermore, Bangor University offered me the option to specialize in Conservation Science, which is the scientific division I am pursuing to work in once I graduate.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The overall university experience is great.  Professors are very welcoming, understanding and down-to-earth.  Furthermore, they're all very active in their scientific divisions and up to date with scientific literature, meaning we were constantly being thought up-to-date topics.  The only downside, and the reason why I did not give a 10 rating, is that the overall course structure isn't very well defined and quite jagged.  However, the university is aware of this and they are actively changing the module structure for next year's intake to make the study flow more consistent.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I would give it a moderate rating.  The university was very helpful in personal email exchanges to explain and give orientation upon arrival.  However, there are some resources (such as an in-depth university campus map outlying the lecture halls) that are non-existent, so there was a lot of confusion in the first couple of weeks till everyone got used to where we needed to go.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I personally did not receive any assistance.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding housing was exceptionally difficult in my experience, because there are very few private landlords offering rent-able apartments/studios to students at an affordable rate.  Best advice I would give is for students to start searching as soon as possible. 

Furthermore, the university is constantly buying more buildings to host/rent to more students.  Please be aware that the prices of the university's dorm rooms are exceptionally higher than some private rent-able options.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
1) Be aware of the location you're renting.  I ended up residing in an apartment in close vicinity to High Street. Noise, especially during the weekends, is so exceptionally loud and obnoxious that it will disrupt sleep.  This might sound minuscule, but in the long term it really does disrupt your exchange experience when you're constantly sleep deprived.

2) Be really careful with the quality of the apartments/studios/rooms you're renting from private landlords.  All my friends, including myself have found dodgy issues in our accommodation, such as low-quality or already broken furniture/items (e.g., faucets & shower heads).

3) Also be aware that renting privately in the UK will generally require a consignor if you wish to pay monthly (an individual that acts like a guarantee that you won't stop paying rent).  If you don't have one, they'll offer you to pre-pay the entire year rent, or make you sign up to private companies that act like a consignor/guarantor (but it will cost you EXTRA per month as a fee).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Registration was initially done online, then we had to go to one of the university buildings for the staff to verify our VISA documents and to pick up the student card, which is required to enter all university buildings.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The only form of assistance available was email communication with the registration department.  In their defense, their replies were always quick and consistent.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In my case, classes were preregistered as part of the exchange and there was no optional modules.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would recommend to get online registration as well as picking up the student card to be done as soon as possible.  Towards the end of registration week, picking up the student card was so busy it took some students in excess of 2-3 hours of waiting to collect them in queue.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: All courses were Level 7 courses based on the UK's course level guidelines.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching was quite different.  At UCPH, most our modules had heavy components of team-work involved ranging from assignments, to presentation or just general group work/group discussions during lectures.  Here in the UK all the lectures where purely the professors speaking with some Q & A interaction with the students.

questions.answer: I would definitely recommend the Conservation Science module to anyone interested in the topic.  The professors that teach it are some of the top researchers in their field, giving exceptionally detailed insight to global issues we're currently facing.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are activities and social clubs for pretty much anything that can come to mind.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend any student to start getting involved with a sports club of their choosing.  It doesn't matter if you're not experienced in it, because there's a variety of different levels to participate in.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would say definitely get into hiking. Northern wales has some of the most stunning landscapes and mountains available in the UK, so if students are free and the weather's good, get out there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: In all honesty, it is not easy.  A large amount of the master students that you'll be studying, are continuing from their B.Sc. in the same institution.  This means the social circles and cliques are already established from their B.Sc.  Furthermore, the local culture is different than that in Denmark, with a lot more informal interactions from strangers, so it is something to get used too.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Definitely try get involved with some forms of social clubs to create connections as you get there.  Then, try attend social events they host to get to know new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I guess it would be the informal social aspect - It's easy to strike conversations with absolute strangers doing any non-academic activity (or vice-versa, be randomly talked too by strangers).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Prepare/sort out accommodation and VISAs as soon as possible, as everything gets filled very fast
2) Be aware Bangor is NOT even remotely close to Copenhagen.  There are very limited activities to do in the village, so you need to fill the rest of the time on your own.
3) The academic aspect is great, but do not forget to go out and experience northern wales as it is stunning.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: In my case, the most rewarding experience is that, apart from meeting exceptionally nice people, I've also managed to establish myself and network within one of the Departments at the University.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge was honestly getting through the winter months.  Weather becomes extremely bad - it is not uncommon to have two-weeks of non-stop rain, meaning you have find ways to entertain yourself, that you might not normally do.
